name: Scarlet
lede: Scarlet is a brilliant red leaning toward orange, named after a medieval luxury cloth that could be any color: the red of kermes and cochineal, of cardinals and redcoats, and of the scarlet woman.

sections.title: A cloth before a color
sections.body:
Scarlet began as a fabric, not a hue. In the German-speaking lands of the eleventh century the word named a very fine, closely shorn woollen cloth, and that cloth could be blue, green or even black [1][7][3]. The best of it was dyed with kermes, the costliest red of the day, and so the name slid from the cloth to the dye and then to the color; by the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries scarlet meant red [1][4][7]. Gage sees the same drift from material to abstract color in purple and perse [5].

Where the word came from is still argued. Pastoureau sets out two candidates: a Persian word that reached Europe through Spanish Arabic *saquirlat*, or the Latin *sigillatus*, sealed, for cloth stamped by the authority that guaranteed its making [4]. The Arabic may itself have come from the Latin, so the question stays open [4]. Either way the word spread across Europe as *escarlata*, *scarlatto* and *Scharlach* [4].

Scarlet is not the only color that started as cloth. Paterson lists russet, Lincoln green and Kendal green among the fabric names that became colors, and khaki as the reverse case, a color that named a cloth [6]. Within the reds the trade kept a working distinction: crimson usually meant a purplish red, scarlet a brighter, more fiery one [3].

sections.title: Kermes: the grain
sections.body:
Medieval scarlet came from an insect. Kermes are tiny scale insects that live on a Mediterranean oak, so small and round that people took them for seeds; Pliny called them a berry that turns into a worm [7][9]. St Clair puts the cost at up to 80 female insects for a single gram of dye [7]. Their trade name was *granum*, grain, which is why a deeply dyed cloth is still called ingrained [8].

The same insect gave English several other words [9][8]. Ball and Paterson trace crimson, carmine and the old French *cramoise* back to kermes [9][8]. The prophet Isaiah's line that sins as red as scarlet shall become white as snow uses scarlet and crimson as the colors of blood [9][10].

Nothing else in the medieval dyer's shop could match it. Pastoureau writes that true textile scarlet could be made only with kermes; madder and orchil, good dyes in their own right, could not reach it [4]. Kermes gave a red that was bright and held fast through light and washing, which is why cloth dyed with it became the model of luxury [7].

sections.title: The price of scarlet
sections.body:
Scarlet was priced out of most people's reach. In the wardrobe accounts of Henry VI of England, even the cheapest scarlet cost nine shillings and fivepence a yard, more than a master mason earned in a month, and the dearest cost twice as much [3][7]. At one Florentine dye shop it cost ten times more to dye cloth an intense *scarlatto* than to dye it sky blue [3]. A fifteenth-century Florentine dyers' manual called crimson the first and highest of all colors [11][12].

The trade was policed hard. The dyers' guild of Lucca, in its statutes of 1255, fined any member caught using cheap red dyestuffs 100 lire or took his right hand [13]. Sumptuary laws in León and Castile reserved scarlet for kings in the thirteenth century, and across much of Europe only the nobility could wear it [7][13]. Venetian scarlet was the envy of the continent; Greenfield floats the idea that its secret was a dash of arsenic, but that is a suggestion, not a finding [3].

Painters recorded the display. Cosimo de' Medici joked that a gentleman could be made with two yards of red cloth, and Pontormo's portrait of him, painted after his death, wraps him in scarlet [3]. Van Dyck kept stock draperies in the studio so that his sitters could appear richer than they were [14].

sections.title: Cochineal and tin
sections.body:
The Spanish conquest of Mexico brought a stronger insect red [15][14]. Cochineal, from a scale insect that feeds on prickly-pear cactus, reached Europe in the sixteenth century [15][18]. In February 1543 six master dyers in Venice tested it on silk against the best kermes crimson and swore it was just as good [14]. Ounce for ounce it was about ten times as strong as kermes [14]. It still took tens of thousands of insects to make a useful amount: Garfield gives about 17,000 per ounce of dye, and Coles about 14,000 for 100 grams of carmine lake [15][16].

The brightest scarlet of all came from cochineal with tin. Around 1606 or 1607, in England, the Dutch inventor Cornelis Drebbel found that tin turned cochineal's dark crimson-purple into a blazing scarlet [17]. Books disagree on how. A popular story says acid spilled onto a tin window frame and dripped into his cochineal by accident; Finlay tells it as fact, St Clair calls it likely apocryphal, and Greenfield doubts it [18][7][17]. Robert Boyle claimed that merchants had set Drebbel to improve a red already found in Holland, though Greenfield finds little evidence for that either [17].

Tin scarlet changed dyeing. A dye house for cochineal was set up at Bow in east London in 1643, and its scarlet became known as Bow dye [15][19]. In Paris, people whispered that the Gobelins dyers had made a pact with the devil to get their red [17]. When the Earl of Essex seized Spanish ships off the Azores in 1597 he took more than 27 tons of cochineal, valued at over 80,000 pounds [20]. British dyeing consumed some 240,000 pounds of cochineal annually by the late eighteenth century, and the East India Company valued it below only gold and silver [21].

sections.title: Cardinals, queens and redcoats
sections.body:
The Church made scarlet its own [3][22]. Books disagree on when: Greenfield says a papal decree of 1295 dressed cardinals in red that was really Byzantine purple, replaced by a European red after Constantinople fell in 1453, while Gage and St Clair credit Pope Paul II in 1464 [3][22][7]. The safe reading is that cardinals took scarlet in the 1460s, when Byzantine purple ran out [3][22].

Monarchs used it with care. Elizabeth I wore scarlet as a princess, but as queen she dressed her attendants in it instead [7]. Shakespeare, as one of the King's players, was issued four and a half yards of scarlet cloth for the coronation of James I [7][23]. Napoleon, urged to revive the silk weavers of Lyon, wore a scarlet taffeta coat embroidered with gold, known as *l'habit rouge* [24].

Soldiers wore it longest. Roman generals wore bright red cloaks [7]. Under Oliver Cromwell, officers' coats were dyed scarlet in Gloucestershire with the new tin recipe, while ordinary soldiers got cheaper madder red [7][17]. Greenfield traces the same scarlet to the coats of the Russian Imperial Guard and the flag over Fort McHenry [17]. British officers' scarlet stayed a cochineal dye into the 1950s; Finlay gives 1952 as the end date and Paterson 1954 [18][25]. The fox-hunter's coat called hunting pink is, Paterson notes, really scarlet [26].

sections.title: The scarlet woman
sections.body:
Scarlet has always carried two meanings. The Book of Revelation dresses the harlot of Babylon in purple and scarlet, and medieval artists often painted her in red [27]. After the Reformation, Puritans pointed to the scarlet of the cardinals as proof that Rome was that harlot [7][3]. Mary, Queen of Scots, wore a scarlet undergown to her execution in 1587: a martyr's color to Catholics, the scarlet woman to her enemies [7].

The nineteenth century cooled on it. During the Terror in France, scarlet gowns became dangerous to wear, and the red of the streets was the cheaper madder of the revolutionary cap [28]. In Britain an 1843 handbook advised respectable women to avoid flaming and gaudy colors, and Hawthorne's *The Scarlet Letter* of 1850 tied the color to adultery [29]. Once synthetic dyes made bright colors cheap in the late 1870s, working people bought magenta and scarlet, and Greenfield argues that the rich turned against bright color altogether [30].

sections.title: Scarlet in the paintbox
sections.body:
Painters had their own scarlets, most of them unreliable. Scarlet lake could mean a cochineal lake, a mixture of crimson lake and vermilion, or iodine scarlet [31]. Iodine scarlet was a bright mercury iodide made after the discovery of iodine, which Humphry Davy named in 1814 [32]. Paterson dates the pigment to 1811 [33]. George Field tested it and judged its beauty almost as short-lived as a scarlet geranium's [32].

Turner almost never used iodine scarlet in oils [32]. The Pigment Compendium explains part of the trouble: mercury iodide exists in a red and a yellow crystal form, and a sample from Turner's own palette contained both [34]. William Mulready used it in *The Widow* of 1823 without disaster, which shows how much depended on preparation [35].

Industry eventually took over the name. Biebrich scarlet, a synthetic dye of 1878 or 1879, was said to rival cochineal in brightness and now survives mainly as a laboratory stain [36]. Medieval scholars had already treated scarlet as the most precious red, putting it, as *coccineus*, where Aristotle's scale of colors had purple [37].

sections.title: Seeing scarlet
sections.body:
Scarlet is a color the eye holds onto. In 1789 Gaspard Monge analysed color constancy, and the Venetian writer Francesco Milizia observed that scarlet still looks scarlet in sunlight, under a blue sky or by artificial light [38]. Goethe, in 1810, described a girl in a scarlet bodice whose afterimage on a white wall was a beautiful sea-green, an early account of color opponency [39]. When writers matched colors to instruments, Gage notes, the pairing that lasted best was scarlet with the trumpet [40].

Werner's mineral color chart, in Syme's edition, defines Scarlet Red as arterial blood red with a little gamboge yellow, and gives as examples the scarlet ibis, the mark on a red grouse's head, the oriental poppy and light red cinnabar [41]. Derek Jarman chose the pelargonium 'Paul Crampel' as the perfect scarlet [42]. Look for it in a geranium bed or a hunting coat: a red pushed toward orange, never toward purple.

sections.title: Which scarlet?
sections.body:
The screen swatch is #FF2400, a red so far toward orange that the ISCC-NBS system calls it vivid reddish orange [43]. It descends from Robert Ridgway's 1886 and 1912 color books, and Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates the color name to 1764 [43]. Its nearest named neighbors are Bright Red, Orangey Red and [[tomato-red]], all under 3.5 units away; [[vermilion]] is 7.2 away and [[crimson]] 15.2 [43].

Old scarlets were darker. Werner's Scarlet Red survives in our library as an aged swatch filed under [[medium-carmine|Medium Carmine]], 16.6 units from the screen color [43]. That fits the history: a kermes or cochineal scarlet on wool was a deep, warm red, not the near-orange glare of a modern display.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, only one has a color within six units of this screen scarlet covering at least five per cent of the canvas: Pierre Bonnard's *[[art:commons-Q17491092|Corner of a Table]]* of 1935 [44]. Photographs of paintings, with their aged varnish, almost never reach a red this pure.

Ridgway's slightly softer plate scarlet finds 26 paintings, and more than half of them, 14, are Indian, about 18 times the archive's rate [44]. Rajput painting carries it 38 times as often as the archive average, led by a 1611 *[[art:cma-314494|Portrait of Prince Sur Singh Rathor of Bikaner]]* where it covers about three fifths of the picture [44]. The earliest European match is a Bramantino *[[art:commons-Q3842513|Madonna and Child and Saints]]* of about 1515 [44].

Werner's darker scarlet is common: 339 paintings, with the 1400s carrying it at almost four times the archive rate [44]. A Sienese panel of 1440, *[[art:rijks-20026322|Payment of Salaries to the Night Watchmen]]*, is more than half this red [44]. As always, these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a color match says nothing about whether the red is kermes, cochineal, vermilion or lac [44]. In Google Books the word *scarlet* peaks in the 1880s and falls to about a fifth of that level by the 1980s [45].

questions.q: Why did the word scarlet come to mean a red?
choices: The luxury wool cloth called scarlet was usually dyed with kermes, so the cloth's name passed to its color
It was named after a red bird
It comes from the Latin word for blood
A pope named the color in 1464
questions.answer: The luxury wool cloth called scarlet was usually dyed with kermes, so the cloth's name passed to its color

questions.q: What turned cochineal's crimson-purple into the brightest scarlet?
